subChunks.title: The Classic Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
subChunks.hookHtml: Genealogical errors are systematic. The same mistakes appear in beginner research everywhere in the world, in every era and every record type. Learning to name them — to recognise them as they happen in your own work — is one of the most valuable things you can do as a developing researcher. Most brick walls are not missing records. They are wrong assumptions that have sent the search in the wrong direction.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The most common genealogical errors

1. Accepting the first finding without corroboration

You find a Patrick Walsh in a census with the right birth year. You copy the information and move on. You have not confirmed this is your Patrick Walsh — you have found a Patrick Walsh. Common surnames (Walsh, Murphy, Smith, Jones, Brown) mean there may be dozens of plausible candidates in a given record set. Every identification must be confirmed by corroborating evidence — another record that connects the same individual to a known fact about your ancestor. One record is a hypothesis. Two independent records pointing to the same conclusion begin to constitute evidence.

2. Same-name confusion

A structural variant of error 1. Multiple people of the same name lived in the same time and place — often in the same family. The classic trap: there are two Thomas Walshes in the county (as we saw in gen-app-8: Junior does not always mean son). You follow the wrong one for three generations and build an extensive tree for a stranger. Diagnostic: when a "family" has a child before the parents were born, or parents were married after the supposed children were born, you have almost certainly merged two families.

3. Assuming surname spelling is fixed

As covered in gen-app-8, historical clerks wrote phonetically. The same family might appear as Walsh, Walshe, Walch, Welsh, or even Welch across different records. Searching only for "Walsh" means missing all the variant spellings. The solution: search by phonetic algorithms (Soundex), browse record images directly, and build a list of variants for every surname you research.

4. Ignoring the calendar

The Julian-to-Gregorian calendar change (England, 14 September 1752) and the associated double-dating problem (January–March dates before 1752) were covered in gen-app-9. A simpler version of this error: the census was taken on a specific date (e.g. 7 June 1841 in England and Wales). A child born on 8 June 1841 will not appear on that census — they did not yet exist on census night. Trying to reconcile that child's birth year with the census will fail. Always know the exact census date.

5. Treating secondary information as primary

The classic form: accepting a birth date from a death certificate as established fact, rather than a secondary estimate requiring corroboration. Any piece of information is only as reliable as the person who provided it and their proximity to the event. A widow reporting her deceased husband's birthdate to the registrar is reporting from memory — secondary information. An eyewitness mother reporting her own newborn's birth date to the registrar is reporting from direct experience — primary information. Same document; different reliability for different facts.

6. Confirmation bias

You have decided your ancestor came from County Cork. You now interpret every ambiguous piece of evidence as confirming County Cork. You ignore evidence that suggests County Clare. The cure: actively look for evidence that contradicts your hypothesis. A researcher who proves their hypothesis is doing genealogy. A researcher who cannot imagine their hypothesis being wrong is doing wishful thinking. Ask yourself: "What would I expect to find if this were false?" Then go and look for those things.

7. Ancestor worship — the celebrity ancestor problem

A published genealogy claims your ancestor was descended from a famous historical figure. You adopt this claim without checking the evidence. Celebrity ancestor claims are disproportionately unverified, often because the proposer had an incentive to find the connection, worked backward from the desired ancestor rather than forward from the proven records, and used authored works (other genealogies) rather than primary sources. If you want to believe you are descended from royalty, you must apply more rigour, not less, to the claimed link — because the further back you go, the thinner the evidence becomes and the more the wishful thinking compounds.

8. Assuming siblings share the same parents

A family in the census has six children. You assume all six have the same biological parents. But the family may include stepchildren from a previous marriage, children of a deceased sibling raised by the family, or (in adoptive arrangements) non-biological children. Remarriage was common in eras of high adult mortality; a 40-year-old widow with three children might marry a widower with two of his own. The census will show them all in the same household with the same head of household. They are not all biological siblings.

9. Misreading date formats

American records use MM/DD/YYYY; British records use DD/MM/YYYY; international records may use YYYY-MM-DD (ISO format). A record showing "3/4/1875" is 3 April in British format and 4 March in American format. This matters most for events near the beginning or end of a year. When the format is ambiguous, note the ambiguity in your research log and look for a corroborating record that removes the ambiguity.

10. Not checking your own citations

You wrote down a source citation and assumed you could find it again. Three months later, you cannot. The film number is missing. The page reference is wrong. The online link has rotted. Good citation practice means recording enough detail that the record can be retrieved independently — not relying on memory or partial references. If you cannot retrieve a record from your own citation, your citation is inadequate.

storyBeats.text: Theodora opens a folder and spreads out three different case files — each with a red annotation across the top. "Three researchers," she says. "Three different trees. Three identical errors."

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: I have been doing this for forty years. The errors are always the same. I do not say this to discourage you — I say it because the errors are predictable, and predictable errors can be anticipated. The one I see most often, the one I call the great destroyer of family trees, is this: accepting the first finding. You find a Patrick Walsh born circa 1820 in the right county — and you move on. But there are six Patrick Walshs born circa 1820 in that county. You have not found your Patrick. You have found a Patrick. He needs a second independent source to confirm he is yours.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: The second error — confirmation bias — is the more dangerous one, because it is invisible to the person committing it. You believe your ancestor came from County Cork. Every ambiguous piece of evidence now looks like evidence for County Cork. The marriage register entry that says 'Ireland' — surely Cork. The passenger list that says 'Cork or Clare' — certainly Cork. You have stopped looking at the evidence and started looking for confirmation. The cure is discipline: every hypothesis you form, ask yourself — what would I expect to find if this were wrong? Then go and look for it.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: And about those celebrity ancestors. I have never once seen a rigorously proven descent from royalty come to me as the first claim of an amateur researcher. They come to me having adopted someone else's published genealogy from the 1890s, worked backward from a king to a yeoman they cannot actually connect, and convinced themselves that the gap in the evidence is just a missing record. The further back the ancestor, the thinner the evidence, and the more the wishful thinking fills the gap. Apply more rigour to famous ancestors, not less.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: One final error that should be taught on day one and almost never is: the date format problem. 3/4/1875. Is that the third of April, as an English record would show? Or the fourth of March, as an American one would? The formats are different. International records add more variation. Always note the format; always look for a corroborating record to confirm ambiguous dates; never assume.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Anchor common errors

Retrieve from memory:

  • Why is finding a person in one record not sufficient to confirm their identity?
  • What is confirmation bias in genealogy, and what is the practical remedy?
  • What can a census household contain that does not mean all members are biological siblings?
  • Why are celebrity ancestor claims particularly prone to error?
  • What date format ambiguity does "3/4/1875" present, and how do you resolve it?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Finding a person in one record is not sufficient because common surnames mean there may be dozens of plausible candidates in a given record set. One record produces a hypothesis; a second independent record pointing to the same individual begins to constitute evidence. The identification is confirmed when multiple independent records all converge on the same person.

Confirmation bias is the tendency to interpret ambiguous evidence as confirming your existing hypothesis while ignoring contradicting evidence. The practical remedy is to actively seek evidence that would falsify your hypothesis: ask 'what would I expect to find if this ancestor did NOT come from Cork?' and then look for those things. If they are absent too, the hypothesis gains strength. If they are present, the hypothesis needs revision.

A census household may contain stepchildren from previous marriages (remarriage was common in eras of high adult mortality), children of deceased siblings raised by the family, or non-biological children in informal adoption arrangements. Not all household members with the same head of household are biological siblings.

Celebrity ancestor claims are particularly prone to error because the proposer often works backward from the desired famous ancestor, uses authored genealogies rather than primary records, and fills gaps in the evidence with wishful thinking. The further back in time, the thinner the primary evidence and the more likely that intermediate generations are assumed rather than proved.

'3/4/1875' is ambiguous: British format = 3 April 1875; American format = 4 March 1875. Resolution: note the country of origin of the record (which format it uses), look for a corroborating record giving the date in a less ambiguous form (e.g. a registration certificate giving the month by name), and record the ambiguity in your research log.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Error identification exercise

Read the following research narrative and identify every methodological error it contains. For each error, name it, explain why it is an error, and suggest the correct approach.

"I found a Thomas Walsh in the 1860 US census in Philadelphia, aged 40, born Ireland. This must be my Thomas Walsh — the ages match and he is from Ireland. His wife is listed as Mary, aged 35, born Ireland. I know my Thomas Walsh married a Mary, so this confirms it. The census also shows five children: Patrick (16), James (12), Bridget (10), Ellen (7), and an infant Michael (1). Thomas is listed as a labourer. I have now proved that my Thomas Walsh's parents were born in Ireland, because the 1880 census for his son Patrick shows both parents born in Ireland. The tree also says Thomas's father was Thomas Walsh Senior, also from Ireland — I found this on an Ancestry family tree."
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Errors identified:

1. Accepting first finding without corroboration. 'This must be my Thomas Walsh — the ages match and he is from Ireland.' A Thomas Walsh aged ~40 born in Ireland in 1860 Philadelphia is not unusual — there are many. Age matching alone is insufficient; a second independent source connecting this Thomas to a known fact about the researcher's ancestor is required.

2. Same-name confirmation via common name. 'His wife is listed as Mary... I know my Thomas Walsh married a Mary, so this confirms it.' The name Mary is extremely common among Irish Catholic immigrants. This is not corroborating evidence — it is another coincidence that needs its own independent confirmation from a marriage record or other document.

3. Assuming all census children are biological. The five children listed are assumed to be Thomas and Mary's biological children. Some may be from Thomas's or Mary's previous marriages, or may be nieces/nephews living in the household.

4. Secondary information treated as settled fact. 'I have now proved that my Thomas Walsh's parents were born in Ireland, because the 1880 census for his son Patrick shows both parents born in Ireland.' The 1880 census question about parents' birthplaces is answered by Patrick — secondary information reported from his recollection of what his parents told him. This is corroborating but not conclusive; it requires a birth or baptism record from Ireland.

5. Authored source cited as evidence. 'The tree also says Thomas's father was Thomas Walsh Senior, also from Ireland — I found this on an Ancestry family tree.' An Ancestry family tree is an authored work. It is not evidence; it is a hypothesis. The researcher must find the underlying primary record (a deed, will, or church record) that established the father's name.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend what confirmation bias means in genealogy — and give a concrete example of how it could lead a researcher to build three generations of the wrong family's tree.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The tendency to favour evidence that confirms an existing hypothesis while discounting or ignoring contradicting evidence — one of the most persistent reasoning errors in genealogical research.
The error of treating two different people with the same name as a single individual, often merging two unrelated family lines into one erroneous tree.
The systematic tendency to overestimate the reliability of claimed descents from famous historical figures, often based on authored genealogies that fill evidential gaps with assumption.
A household formed by the remarriage of a widowed or divorced parent, often containing children from multiple relationships — a common source of sibling misidentification in census records.
The GPS standard requiring that a researcher search all record types that might reasonably contain relevant information, not only the convenient or already-online sources.

questions.questionHtml: What does it mean, in genealogical terms, to commit the error of accepting the first finding?
options: Treating the first matching record found as confirmed identification of your ancestor without seeking corroborating evidence from a second independent source
Starting research with the most recent generation rather than working backward
Searching only one database instead of multiple platforms
Accepting an index entry as a substitute for viewing the original record image
questions.correctAnswer: Treating the first matching record found as confirmed identification of your ancestor without seeking corroborating evidence from a second independent source
questions.explanationHtml: When a common-surname ancestor appears in a record that matches known facts (right name, right approximate age, right location), the temptation is to accept the identification immediately. But there may be many plausible candidates. One matching record produces a hypothesis; a second independent record pointing to the same individual begins to constitute evidence. Only when multiple independent sources converge on the same person is the identification reasonably secure.

questions.questionHtml: You discover that a census shows a family with two sons named "John" — one aged 15 and one aged 3. What is the most plausible genealogical explanation?
options: The first John died in infancy and the name was reused for the second child — reuse of a given name in the same family generation almost always indicates the earlier child's death
The younger John is a step-sibling with the same name by coincidence
The census enumerator made a clerical error and one of the Johns is actually a Jane
Both Johns were the same person listed twice due to a census counting error
questions.correctAnswer: The first John died in infancy and the name was reused for the second child — reuse of a given name in the same family generation almost always indicates the earlier child's death
questions.explanationHtml: When a family has two children with the same given name in the same generation (e.g. two Johns twelve years apart), the near-universal explanation is that the first child died before the second was born and the name was reused — either to honour the lost child or to pass on the name of the grandparent after whom the first John was named. A search for the first John's burial record between his birth and the second John's birth will almost always confirm the death. This is one of the naming-convention signals covered in gen-app-8.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher finds an elaborate published genealogy from 1912 claiming descent from a 14th-century Irish chieftain through 22 generations. The researcher immediately adds all 22 generations to their tree, citing the 1912 publication. What is wrong with this approach, and what should they do instead?
options: Published genealogies are authored works; the 1912 publication's claims must be checked against primary sources generation by generation — the further back the claimed descent, the thinner the evidence, and the greater the risk of assumption filling evidential gaps; each generation should be independently proved from contemporary records before being accepted
Published genealogies from before 1950 are automatically invalid
The researcher should add the generations but mark them as 'unverified' — that is sufficient caution
14th-century records do not exist anywhere, so such a descent cannot be verified or disproved and may simply be accepted
questions.correctAnswer: Published genealogies are authored works; the 1912 publication's claims must be checked against primary sources generation by generation — the further back the claimed descent, the thinner the evidence, and the greater the risk of assumption filling evidential gaps; each generation should be independently proved from contemporary records before being accepted
questions.explanationHtml: A published genealogy is an authored work whose quality depends entirely on the evidence its author used and cited. A 1912 publication predates the Genealogical Proof Standard and may rest on oral tradition, other genealogies, wishful thinking, or plain invention. Checking 22 generations of claimed descent from the 14th century requires working backward record by record through church registers, wills, deeds, and administrative records — a formidable but not impossible task for well-documented families. Adding all 22 generations without checking is the celebrity-ancestor problem in practice: you have built 22 potentially wrong generations into your tree and may now never be able to remove them because they have become embedded. The correct procedure is to start from the proved family and work backward one generation at a time, each step independently documented.
